verses.text: Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying, “Keep all the commandment which I command you today.
It shall be on the day when you shall pass over the Jordan to the land which Yahweh your God gives you, that you shall set yourself up great stones, and coat them with plaster.

You shall write on them all the words of this law, when you have passed over; that you may go in to the land which Yahweh your God gives you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as Yahweh, the God of your fathers, has promised you.
It shall be, when you have crossed over the Jordan, that you shall set up these stones, which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall coat them with plaster.
There you shall build an altar to Yahweh your God, an altar of stones. You shall not use any iron tool on them.
You shall build Yahweh your God’s altar of uncut stones. You shall offer burnt offerings on it to Yahweh your God.
You shall sacrifice peace offerings, and shall eat there. You shall rejoice before Yahweh your God.
You shall write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly.”
Moses and the priests the Levites spoke to all Israel, saying, “Be silence, and listen, Israel! Today you have become the people of Yahweh your God.
You shall therefore obey Yahweh your God’s voice, and do his commandments and his statutes, which I command you today.”
Moses commanded the people the same day, saying,
“These shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, when you have crossed over the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
These shall stand on Mount Ebal for the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.
With a loud voice, the Levites shall say to all the men of Israel,
‘Cursed is the man who makes an engraved or molten image, an abomination to Yahweh, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and sets it up in secret.’ All the people shall answer and say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who dishonors his father or his mother.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who removes his neighbor’s landmark.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who leads the blind astray on the road.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who withholds justice from the foreigner, fatherless, and widow.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who lies with  his father’s wife, because he dishonors his father’s bed.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who lies with any kind of animal.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who lies with his sister, his father’s daughter or his mother’s daughter.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who lies with his mother-in-law.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who secretly kills his neighbor.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who takes a bribe to kill an innocent person.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
‘Cursed is he who doesn’t uphold the words of this law by doing them.’ All the people shall say, ‘Amen.’”

footnotes.content: Moses stands at the edge of the Jordan with all the weight of forty years behind him, and now he speaks with the elders—the keepers and witnesses of the law. 'Keep all the commandment,' he says. Not most of it, not when it's convenient. All of it. This is what love for God's people looks like: clarity without apology.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first thing they'll do when they cross the Jordan is not plant crops or build houses—it's to erect great stones and coat them with plaster. The Lord knows we need something tangible to hold onto, something that stands. Words carved in stone last longer than words in the heart, don't they? Both matter, but stones remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Write the *words of the law* on those stones—not a summary, not the highlights, but the law itself. So that when Israelites walk the land and their children ask 'Why do we do these things?' they can point to Gerizim and read the answer carved in stone. The law is not secret; it's public witness to who God is and what He expects.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mount Ebal. The mountain of curse, not blessing. These stones go there—where the blessings will *not* naturally gather, where the hard truths are spoken aloud. The Lord insists we face both mountains: blessing and consequence. He will not let us pretend one doesn't exist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An altar of stones, no iron tool to shape them. The Lord wants His altar made of what the earth gives, unaltered by human craft. There's a quiet rebuke here—we tend to improve on God's design, to polish and refine everything until it bears our thumbprint. But worship works best when we show up empty-handed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uncut stones, burnt offerings rising up. This is the first act of settled worship in the Promised Land—not after the harvest, not after comfort, but immediately, with whole devotion. The Lord does not wait for convenience. Neither do His covenant people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peace offerings and rejoicing—the meal, the community gathered, joy before Yahweh. Sacrifice without celebration is half-finished. The Lord invites us to *feast*, to look around at the faces around the table and say: this is our covenant people, and we are glad.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Very plainly. Not in code, not in riddles, not for scholars alone. A shepherd, a child, a weary traveler—all of them should be able to read what's written and understand what God requires. Grace is not obscure; it is written *very plainly*, and we all have permission to read it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and the priests stand together and say: 'Be silent and listen.' The moment is solemn. Not fearful—Christ has not yet come—but aware that something sacred is happening. And then the announcement: 'Today you have become the people of Yahweh your God.' Not tomorrow, not eventually. Today. The covenant is active, present tense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obey His voice. Do His commandments and statutes. Now—not after you've figured everything out, not when it makes sense, not when you feel like it. Now, as a covenant people. Obedience comes first; understanding grows along the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses commands the people—another command, but this one prepares them for what comes next. A ceremonial act. A physical staging that makes the invisible visible: the choice between blessing and curse stands before them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mount Gerizim, the tribes of blessing: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin. Six tribes stand here. The Lord assigns which tribes represent blessing—not arbitrary, but tied to each tribe's calling and role. Levi stands here because they are the priests. Joseph because his line carries the promise. The mountains teach through flesh and blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mount Ebal, the tribes of curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali. The Lord makes no one *inherently* cursed, but He appoints these six tribes to stand where curses are declared. This is ceremony, not fate—each person still chooses obedience or rebellion. The mountains hold the words; human hearts hold the choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Levites speak with a loud voice—not whispered, not private. The curses are proclaimed openly so that all Israel hears and knows what rebellion costs. There is no hiding from the law; it is written and spoken in daylight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first curse: engraved or molten images, the work of human hands, set up in secret. Idolatry thrives in darkness. The Lord insists on truth and light. When we craft gods to suit ourselves—in secret, in shadow—we invite curse. And the people answer 'Amen'—they pledge to this rejection, binding themselves to monotheism.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cursed is he who dishonors father or mother. Even here, on the brink of nationhood, the Lord roots covenant in the family. To dishonor parents is to dishonor the order God Himself made. Honor costs something; dishonor costs more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Removing a neighbor's landmark—boundary stones that mark what belongs to whom. A quiet theft, almost invisible. But the Lord sees and names it. Justice whispers sometimes; we must listen for it. Property rights, dignity, honesty in measurement and deed—all sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leading the blind astray on the road. The blind person trusts you to know the way. To betray that trust is to prey on vulnerability. The Lord marks it. He will not have cruelty to the helpless tolerated, and neither should we.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Withholding justice from the foreigner, fatherless, widow—those with no voice, no advocate. Again and again, the law circles back to these three. They are God's concern, and if Israel ignores them, Israel ignores the Lord Himself. Mercy to the weak is not optional charity; it is covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lying with his father's wife—a betrayal of family bond and sexual integrity. The law does not hide from hard realities; it names them. Some paths lead to curse because they dishonor what God has made sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lying with any kind of animal—distortion of the order of creation. The Lord made us male and female, made animals for us, but not *with* us. Some boundaries protect our humanity itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sister, father's daughter, mother's daughter—incest dissolves the family bonds that hold society together. The law is clear because civilization depends on these boundaries. We blur them at our peril.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mother-in-law. Even extended family carries the sacred trust. Sex is not a neutral act; it binds people and implies loyalty. The law protects that bond.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Secretly kills his neighbor—murder done in shadow, hoping no one will know. But the Lord sees. Hidden sins carry their own curse; we cannot escape His eye. Light breaks into darkness sooner or later.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Taking a bribe to kill an innocent—the law names the worst kind of cruelty: selling a human life for money. Justice for sale is not justice; it is corruption of the highest order. The Lord abhors it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cursed is he who doesn't uphold the words of this law by doing them. Readers today hear an echo here—none of us uphold the law perfectly, and the curse falls on all of us. But that's precisely why Jesus came: to bear the curse we deserved, to write a new covenant in His blood. The law reveals our need; grace meets it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
